implementation_notes: Kotlin contributes the suspend keyword, which the compiler turns into a state machine, but the machinery that resumes suspended coroutines lives in kotlinx.coroutines: builders such as launch and async, the dispatcher that decides which threads run resumptions, and the structured-concurrency scope that owns their lifetimes. I/O itself is usually a JVM blocking or NIO.2 API wrapped by the library (Dispatchers.IO) or an asynchronous client, so the completion dispatcher is the dispatcher's thread pool rather than an explicit event loop; the raw CompletionHandler form is justified only when integrating NIO.2 channels directly.
pitfalls: Blocking calls that are not moved to Dispatchers.IO occupy a core dispatcher thread and stall every coroutine sharing it.
Cancellation is cooperative: a coroutine that never suspends or checks isActive keeps running after cancel.
launch on GlobalScope breaks structured concurrency and leaks work past its owner's lifetime; use a scope tied to the component.
Dispatchers.IO has a 64-thread default bound shared process-wide, so a burst of blocking work can starve other components.
